title: Working with Long COVID — Warehouse Shift Supervisor (Darren Fletcher)
transcript:
[00:00:05] INT: Okay, the recorder is running now. So, thank you again for agreeing to take part in the Working with Long COVID study here with the Northshire Health Research Group at the University of Northshire. Just to double-check before we start, you're happy for me to record this?
[00:00:21] P: Yeah, yeah, totally fine, Chloe. Fire away.
[00:00:25] INT: Brilliant. So, to kick things off, could you tell me a little bit about yourself and what your working life looked like before you got ill?
[00:00:34] P: Right, well, I'm Darren—Darren Fletcher. I'm fifty-one, born the 3rd of May 1973, and I live just off 42 Alder Grove, up on the Millfield estate in Brampton-on-Trent. Before all this kicked off, I was a warehouse shift supervisor at Pennine Freight & Logistics Ltd, over on the Marston Industrial Park. Been there nearly fourteen years, worked my way up from the loading bays. I ran B-Shift Despatch—about eighteen lads and lasses under me. It was proper physical work, twelve-hour shifts, four on, four off. I loved it, honestly. I was actually the only supervisor on site certified to operate and troubleshoot the V-Lift 4000 automated vertical-lift pallet cranes, so I felt pretty indispensable, you know? If one of those jammed at three in the morning, it was my phone ringing. Outside of work, I was always on the go. I've got a workshop in the garage where I build 1:16 scale live-steam traction engines from scratch—machining the brass myself and all that. Haven't touched the lathe in over a year now, though.
[00:01:52] INT: That sounds like a really skilled job and a brilliant hobby. Can you take me back to when you first caught COVID and how things changed?
[00:02:03] P: Yeah, I remember the exact date because it was right before our busy Christmas run—14th of November 2022. I tested positive on the Monday morning. Thought I'd be back in a week, maybe ten days. I mean, I've had mild asthma since I was a kid, used a Ventolin inhaler now and then, so I wasn't expecting a walk in the park, but I wasn't expecting this. The actual virus knocked me sideways for about three weeks, and then... I just never bounced back. By January 2023, I was still getting this crushing fatigue. Not just tired like after a double shift, you know? It's like somebody's poured wet concrete into your veins. And the shortness of breath—I'd walk up the stairs at home and have to sit on the landing for ten minutes with my heart hammering out of my chest.
[00:03:04] INT: Did you go to your GP around that time?
[00:03:08] P: Yeah, I went to Oakwood Medical Practice and saw Dr. Helen Osei. To be fair to her, she was brilliant. She didn't fob me off like some of the stories you hear. She ran bloods, did an ECG, and said, 'Darren, this looks like Long COVID.' She referred me to the Long COVID Rehab Clinic at St. Jude's General Hospital. Mind you, the waiting list was a joke. They actually lost my referral twice! I remember sitting on hold for forty-five minutes reading out my NHS number—999 482 7105—just trying to prove I existed. I didn't actually get seen by Dr. Alan Bradshaw at St. Jude's until July 2023.
[00:03:56] INT: That's a really long wait while you're feeling so unwell. What happened when you did see Dr. Bradshaw?
[00:04:04] P: Well, he did a stand test and diagnosed me with POTS—Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome—alongside the Long COVID and Post-Exertional Malaise. Basically, if I push through and do too much one day, I'm flat on my back for the next four days with chest tightness, joint pain, and this awful brain fog. He put me on Ivabradine for the heart palpitations, and Dr. Osei later added 10mg of Amitriptyline at night to help with the nerve pain and sleep. The brain fog is honestly the scariest bit, Chloe. I've always had a sharp head for numbers and stock manifests. Now, I'll walk into the kitchen and forget why I'm there, or I'll be mid-sentence talking to my wife Sandra and the word just vanishes.
[00:04:58] INT: How did you handle talking to your employer about all of this?
[00:05:04] P: [sighs] At first, I kept it quiet, didn't I? Because in a warehouse, you don't want to look weak. I told my operations manager, Gareth Pritchard, that I was just taking a bit longer to shake off a chest infection. When I finally went back in March 2023 on a phased return, I lasted four days. On the fourth day, I was trying to log a damaged pallet on the system—something I've done a thousand times—and I just stared at the screen. Couldn't process it. My mate Dave Kowalski, who's a team leader on B-Shift, found me leaning against the racking, shaking and drenched in sweat. He literally drove me home.
[00:05:51] INT: That must have been terrifying. What happened after that?
[00:05:56] P: I went back off sick, and that's when HR got involved. A woman called Priya Nair. Suddenly it wasn't 'how are you feeling, Darren?' anymore, it was formal absence review meetings. I gave them the letter from St. Jude's General Hospital explaining the Long COVID and POTS. I asked for workplace adjustments—could I move to a seated role in the goods-in office, maybe drop the night shifts, do twenty hours a week? Gareth just looked at me across the table and said, 'Pennine Freight is a twenty-four-hour operation, Darren, we can't invent a desk job for you.' Even when I brought my rep from the Midlands Transport & Warehouse Union—the MTWU—they didn't budge.
[00:06:48] INT: So they wouldn't consider any redeployment at all?
[00:06:53] P: Nothing. They said my capability to do my contracted role wasn't going to improve in a 'reasonable timeframe.' That was their favourite phrase. On the 18th of October 2023, they dismissed me on medical capability grounds. Fourteen years, employee ID PF-88412, and they packed my locker into a cardboard box and posted it to me. [laughs dryly] Didn't even get a card.
[00:07:24] INT: I'm so sorry, Darren. That sounds brutal after giving so many years to a company. How has that affected you financially?
[00:07:35] P: Oh, it's been a complete disaster. At Pennine Freight, I was earning £34,500 a year. With overtime, we were comfortable, you know? When I went off sick, I dropped straight down to Statutory Sick Pay—£109.40 a week. You can't pay a £980 a month mortgage on that. We burned through our savings in six months. Now I'm on Universal Credit. My claim ref is UC-9042-771B, I've got it memorised because I'm always having to ring them. I'm getting the standard allowance of £393.45 a month while I wait for my Work Capability Assessment to see if I get the LCWRA element. I have to go down to Brampton Jobcentre every couple of weeks, and half the time the walk from the bus stop wipes me out for the weekend. We've racked up £4,200 on credit cards just buying groceries and keeping the heating on.
[00:08:38] INT: That's an enormous amount of pressure on top of managing a chronic illness. How has it affected your family and your sense of who you are?
[00:08:48] P: [pause] Yeah, it's... it's hard. My wife, Sandra, she works part-time at a primary school, and she's had to pick up extra cleaning shifts just to keep us afloat. I hate it. I've always been the provider, the bloke who fixes things. Now I'm sitting on the sofa in my joggers while she's knackered. It causes arguments, obviously—not because she's nasty, she's a saint, really, it's just the stress. Our kids are older—Callum's twenty-four and lives over in Leeds, and Megan's nineteen, she's still at home doing her college course. Megan's brilliant, she helps out loads, brings me cups of tea when I'm having a bad POTS day, but she shouldn't have to be looking after her dad at nineteen. I just feel like a ghost of myself, Chloe. Like Darren the supervisor died in November 2022 and left this bloke behind who can't even walk the dog.
[00:09:56] INT: It sounds like you're grieving a whole version of your life. Before we wrap up, is there anything you wish employers or doctors understood better about working with Long COVID?
[00:10:10] P: I think... just believe us, you know? Just because I don't have a leg in plaster doesn't mean I'm swinging the lead. If Pennine Freight had given me a bit of flexibility—a chair, shorter shifts, a bit of patience—I could still be contributing. Instead, they binned me off, and now the state's paying me a pittance while I'm stuck in limbo. And for the doctors, well, Dr. Osei was great, but waiting seven months for a clinic when your job's on the line? It's too late by then.
[00:10:48] INT: Thank you so much for being so open with me today, Darren. I'll stop the recording in a second, but just so I can send over your thank-you voucher and the summary of the transcript, could you confirm your best email and phone number?
[00:11:02] P: Yeah, sure. Email is darren.fletcher73@example.com, and my mobile is 07700 900418. Just text me if I don't answer, because sometimes I'm having a nap in the afternoon.
[00:11:16] INT: Got it. Thank you again, Darren. I'll switch off now.
